question: When machines were repeatedly promised to replace human translators and interpreters, as in 1954 and 1966, what actually happened to the people doing the work, and which part of it stays with people and for how long?

issues.note: Hard cut from the translation-editor desk to the library street. The opening question narration ends right on the cut, and the film then jumps to a lamplighter with no link to translators.
The narration about volunteers shifts to a library reading room that does not read as the Red Cross translators. It then cuts to archival-style photos, a sudden change of look.
The narration jumps from the 1942 Red Cross archival photos to a 3D Nuremberg courtroom. The change of look is abrupt, and the picture stays nearly static across the cut.
The narration reads 'ready within a few years. In 1966,' and the picture jumps from the 1954 computer room to a 1966 office with a dissolve. This is acceptable, but the narration's tail is cut off.
The narration says 'The results were thin' over a quote card, then a close-up of the typewriter in a different framing. The sequence of pictures is hard to follow.
A split-screen comparison of 1966 and today sits over the narration 'now: part of the job', then it cuts abruptly to a wide shot of an unrelated office. The wide shot does not match the narration.
The quote 'cannot yet' is repeated over the same shot, then cuts to the 1966 paper close-up. The return to the comparison is slightly disorienting.
Several consecutive frames show the same dark courtroom interpreter booths, with little new to see.
The same translation-editor desk close-up is held from R14.1 to R14.5, with small changes only in the captions.
The same translator office is held across several frames, with captions only; this stretch starts at the T12 split.
The video-call interpreter shot is held for a long time with static statistics, and the same visual idea repeats.
